parts.title: Notices around Hartwell
parts.instructions: For each notice, choose what it means.
notices: HARTWELL LIBRARY: The Wi-Fi password changes every Monday. Please ask at the desk for the new one, or look for the card on the notice board.
PHONE DOCTOR, MARKET LANE: Screen repairs at half the usual price this week only. You do not need to book. Just bring your phone and your charger.
TEGID: I left my grey phone charger in the cafe on Friday. Has anyone seen it? I am at work until six, so text me, please. Do not call.
LEARNING CENTRE: Please book a computer at the desk before you sit down. Sessions last one hour, but you can stay longer if nobody is waiting.
COLLEGE IT NOTICE: The system will update tonight between 10 p.m. and midnight. Save your work and log out before you leave, or you may lose it.

parts.title: A week without social media
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last month my cousin told me I spent too much time on my phone, and I laughed. Then she challenged me to stay off social media for a whole week, and I said yes before I could change my mind.

On the first day I kept picking up my phone to check things that were not there. I looked at the screen on the bus, in the queue at the shop, even in the middle of conversations. By Wednesday I was checking much less, and the week felt easier. I read half a book, which I had not done for months, and I cooked a proper dinner instead of watching videos while I ate.

The hardest part was not the free time. It was the messages. My friends use a group chat to plan everything, and I missed an invitation to a birthday meal because nobody phoned me. When I told them, they were surprised and a little sorry. We agreed that anything important would be sent to me by text as well.

At the end of the week I did not delete my accounts. I like seeing what my friends are doing, and I use the internet to learn new things. But now I put my phone on silent in the evening, and I leave my phone in another room when I go to bed. I am not sure my cousin was completely right about me, but I sleep better than I used to.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer accept the challenge?
options: She wanted to prove that her cousin was wrong.
She wanted to spend more time with her cousin.
She agreed quickly without thinking much.
She had already decided to leave social media.
questions.explanation: She says she said yes before she could change her mind, so she agreed quickly.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel by Wednesday?
options: She was bored with her free time.
questions.explanation: By Wednesday she was checking her phone much less and the week felt easier.

questions.prompt: What problem did she have with her friends?
options: They were angry about the challenge.
They stopped using the group chat.
questions.explanation: She missed an invitation to a birthday meal because nobody phoned her.

questions.prompt: What did her friends agree to do?
options: Send her important news by text too.
questions.explanation: They agreed that anything important would be sent to her by text as well.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel about social media now?
options: She should stop using it completely.
It is useful if she controls it.
It is the main reason she cannot sleep.
questions.explanation: She kept her accounts because she likes them, but she puts her phone on silent in the evening.

parts.title: A town app for bus times
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Hartwell is a small town with a big problem: the buses never seem to come when the timetable says they will. Passengers used to stand in the cold, not knowing whether the number 12 had already gone. [1] Last spring, a group of students from the college decided to change that.

They started by sitting at bus stops and writing down the real arrival times for six weeks. [2] With that information, they built a simple app that shows where each bus is on a map.

The app was ready by September, but the students needed help from the bus company. [3] He liked it at once and agreed to share the live position of every bus.

The app went live in November. [4] The students say that the best comments come from older passengers, who now stay at home until the bus is nearly at their stop.

Of course, the app is not perfect. Sometimes the signal is weak and the map shows a bus in the wrong place. [5] The team reads every report and fixes problems within a few days.
sentences: They discovered that many morning buses were ten minutes late or more.
Most of them had never written a computer program before.
Users can report these mistakes with one button.
The first bus of the day leaves the station at five.
The company also sells tickets on its website.
Within a month, more than a thousand people had downloaded it.
So they asked to meet the manager and show him a first version.
Some of them gave up on the bus completely.

gaps.explanation: “Some of them” refers to the passengers who stood in the cold, and the next sentence moves on to the students who wanted to “change that”.
After writing down real arrival times, the students discovered that buses were late; “that information” in the next sentence refers to this discovery.
They needed help from the bus company, so they met the manager; “He” in the next sentence is the manager and “it” is the first version of the app.
“Within a month” continues from “went live in November”, and “it” is the app. The next sentence talks about comments from users.
“These mistakes” refers to the bus shown in the wrong place, and “every report” in the next sentence links to the report button.

parts.title: Buying a new laptop
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: My old laptop had become so slow that I finally decided to buy a new one. I wanted something light enough to [1] to college every day, so I spent a week reading reviews. I looked at several websites to [2] prices and found two I liked. There was a special [3] on laptops that week, so I went to the shop on Saturday. I paid by card, and the laptop was [4] to my house two days later. It was easy to set up, and the battery [5] much longer than my old one. I am really [6] with it.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: You carry a light laptop to college; you do not hold, wear or hang it every day.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: To compare prices means to look at several prices and see which is best.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: An offer is a special price for a short time; a gift or prize is free and a bill is something you pay.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: A shop delivers goods to a house; the laptop was delivered, not collected or ordered, by the shop.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: A battery lasts a long or a short time; stays, stands and keeps do not fit before “much longer than”.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: The adjective “pleased” is followed by “with”; the other adjectives take different prepositions.

parts.title: A message about a video call
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Chase,
Thanks for your message. Sorry I [1] answer the call yesterday evening. I was [2] the train and the signal was very weak. Can we try again on Sunday? I never wake up early on Sundays, so any time [3] ten o’clock is fine for me. Please remember to [4] on your microphone, because last time I could not hear you [5] all. If it still does not work, we can just send voice messages [6] of talking live.
Bye for now,
Tyler

gaps.explanation: A past action that did not happen needs a negative past form: “Sorry I didn’t answer”.
We say “on the train” for being a passenger on public transport.
He never wakes up early, so any time after ten o’clock suits him.
“Turn on” or “switch on” a microphone means to start it.
“Not … at all” is a fixed phrase meaning “not in any way”.
“Instead of” means “in place of”: voice messages in place of talking live.

parts.title: Short conversations about technology
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: tendai
turns.text: Hello, how can I help you?

turns.speaker: emilia
turns.text: My phone fell on the floor yesterday. At first I thought the camera was broken, because there’s a dark mark on every photo.

turns.speaker: tendai
turns.text: Let me see. No, the camera is fine. Have you tried charging it? The charger socket is often the problem after a fall.

turns.speaker: emilia
turns.text: Yes, it charges well. The dark mark is just the long crack in the glass, and in one corner the touch doesn’t work.

turns.speaker: tendai
turns.text: Ah, I see it now. So it’s the screen. We can replace it in two days, and it costs eighty pounds.

turns.speaker: emilia
turns.text: That’s fine. I’ll leave it with you.

question.prompt: What does the woman need to have repaired?
question.explanation: The camera and the charger socket work well; the dark mark and the touch problem come from the cracked screen.

turns.speaker: salma
turns.text: My phone dies by lunchtime. I’m thinking of buying a better one, but they’re so expensive.

turns.speaker: anton
turns.text: Don’t. Yours is only two years old. The battery is the problem, not the phone. A new battery costs about twenty pounds at the shop on Bridge Street.

turns.speaker: salma

turns.speaker: anton
turns.text: You told me there are no sockets near your desk, so that won’t help. Just change the battery.

turns.speaker: jenna

The red one is thirty pounds cheaper, and honestly I love the look of the red one, it’s gorgeous. parts.title: A talk about a tech club
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: speaker-1
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Hartwell Tech Club. I’m Kyle, and I’m going to tell you about our new series of workshops, which starts next month. We meet every Wednesday evening. We tried Thursdays last year, but too many members had other plans, so we moved. The workshops take place in the community hall, behind the bus station. It’s a big, bright room, and it has very good wi-fi. Please don’t go to the library, as some people did last time, and then wait outside the wrong door for twenty minutes. Each session lasts ninety minutes, from seven o’clock until half past eight. We tried two hours at the beginning, but people were tired, and the last half hour was not very useful. In the first workshop we will learn how to build a website. You don’t need any experience at all, just a little curiosity and some patience. In the second one, we’ll make a simple game, and later in the series we’ll have a session on photo editing. If you can, please bring headphones, because we watch some short videos and the room gets noisy. You don’t need to bring a laptop, because we have ten that you can use, but you are welcome to bring your own. Finally, the cost. At my old club, each session was ten pounds, but ours is cheaper. Each session costs five pounds, which pays for the room and for the tea and the biscuits. Students pay the same. If you come to all ten sessions, the last one is free. You can pay at the door, in cash, or by card. Now, are there any questions before we start? If not, please help yourselves to a biscuit and a cup of tea.

gaps.explanation: Thursdays were tried last year, but now they meet on Wednesday evenings.

gaps.prompt: The workshops are in the community ___, behind the bus station
gaps.explanation: They are in the community hall, not in the library.
Each session lasts ninety minutes; two hours was too long.

gaps.prompt: In the first workshop, members will learn to build a ___
gaps.explanation: The first workshop is about building a website; the game comes second.

gaps.prompt: Members should bring ___ if they can
gaps.explanation: He asks for headphones; a laptop is not needed.

parts.title: An interview with a web designer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Aaliyah, how did you begin designing websites?

turns.speaker: aaliyah
turns.text: I didn’t study it. I did a year of design at college, but that was graphic design, posters mostly. And I never answered an advert. A friend of mine ran a football team, and the old website was terrible, so I said I’d try. I watched videos for two weeks and built it. Everybody liked it, and that’s how I got my first clients.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What do you do first with a new customer?

turns.speaker: aaliyah
turns.text: Many designers show examples and colours first, but I like to start with questions. Who is going to visit the website, and what do they need? A bakery customer wants opening hours and a menu, nothing else, and a map so people can find the door. The colours and the pictures come later. If you don’t know what visitors need, it doesn’t matter how pretty the page looks.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What’s the most common mistake on websites?

turns.speaker: aaliyah
turns.text: Too many words on one page. People want to tell everything about themselves. Small pictures happen sometimes, and long names are a problem for some, but the biggest one is a wall of text. Nobody reads it. I once saw a page with two thousand words about the history of a plumber’s family, and I wanted to cry. I tell my customers, fewer words and bigger headings.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why must a page load quickly?

turns.speaker: aaliyah
turns.text: It isn’t about money. A quick page costs the same to build. And phones can show long pages with no trouble. The real reason is patience. If a page takes more than three seconds, people leave. They go back to the search and click on another one. I test every page on a slow phone, to see what a normal visitor sees.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you feel about the changes in your job?

turns.speaker: aaliyah
turns.text: I’m not afraid, though some friends are. The new tools save me hours every week, so I use them every day. I’m not planning to stop designing, I love it. Clients still need somebody who understands people, so I think there will always be work for me. What I enjoy most is the moment when a customer sees the finished page and says, that’s exactly what I wanted.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What advice would you give?

turns.speaker: aaliyah
turns.text: Don’t study for years before you start, you’ll learn faster by doing. Reading about famous designers is nice, but it won’t teach you much. Choose a small project, like a page for your cousin’s shop, and finish it. The first one will be bad, and the second will be better. Mine was terrible, and I’m still a little embarrassed when I remember it.

questions.prompt: What is the most common mistake on websites?
options: Putting too many words on a page.
Using pictures that are too small.

questions.explanation: Small pictures and long names happen, but the biggest mistake is a wall of text.
